q: A vendor's ADT feed uses an unusual character in place of the usual pipe, and a new receiving parser splits every segment incorrectly. What must the parser read first to split the message correctly?
opts: The delimiter setting negotiated during the MLLP connection handshake
The version number in the header, which maps each release to a fixed delimiter set
The opening characters of the MSH segment, where the message declares its own punctuation
The first PID segment, whose layout reveals the separator pattern in use
why: MSH always comes first and its opening characters (the field separator, then the encoding characters) tell the parser how to split everything after it. MLLP has no handshake that negotiates delimiters; it only frames the message with start and end block characters. The declared version does not fix a delimiter set, since senders may legally choose their own. PID cannot be parsed at all until the delimiters are already known.

q: Registration fixes a misspelled surname and an outdated phone number for a patient who is still admitted in the same bed. Which ADT trigger event should the feed send so downstream systems pick up the correction?
opts: A02, transfer to a new location
A08, update patient information
A11, cancel a prior admit
A03, discharge from the encounter
why: A08 is the update-patient-information event: demographics changed, but the visit's location and status did not. A02 announces a location change, which did not happen here. A11 would tell receivers to undo the admission entirely, and A03 would end the encounter. Sending a wrong trigger event can move a patient's bed or close a visit in downstream systems.

q: An EHR places a lab order through an engine, and the lab later returns an ORU result. The EHR must attach the result to the right open order. What does it match on?
opts: The control ID from the original order message's header, repeated in the result message
The placer order number it assigned, echoed back alongside the lab's own filler number
The set ID on the observation segment, which the EHR assigned when it created the order
The visit number alone, since a visit never has more than one open order
why: The ordering system (placer) assigns a placer order number, the fulfilling system (filler) assigns its own, and the result echoes both so the order can be matched. The header control ID identifies one message for acknowledgment purposes and is not repeated as an order key. The OBX set ID is only a sequence number within a single message. A visit routinely has many orders, so the visit number cannot identify one.

q: A sender's log shows a well-formed ADT message was delivered over MLLP and came back with an acknowledgment code of AE plus error text. What is the most accurate reading?
opts: The receiver evaluated the message and hit an application error, so an identical resend will likely fail again
The receiver refused the message outright because its version is unsupported, so it was never evaluated
The receiver accepted the message and will report the final outcome in a later, separate acknowledgment
The reply was lost on the network, so the sender should treat the delivery outcome as unknown for now
why: AE means the receiving application got the message, evaluated it, and failed during processing, so a blind resend repeats the failure until the data or mapping is fixed. Outright refusal before evaluation is the AR pattern. A later separate acknowledgment is how enhanced acknowledgment mode works, and it would not use an error code now. A lost reply produces a timeout, not a coded response with error text.

q: A CIO proposes replacing every HL7 v2 interface with FHIR APIs in a single project. Which consideration most strongly supports a phased approach that keeps v2 running for some systems?
opts: FHIR resources cannot represent orders, results, or admissions in any structured form
Certification rules prohibit decommissioning any v2 interface once it has gone into production use
Many analyzers and monitors only emit v2, so each needs vendor work or a translating layer first
FHIR APIs cannot use the OAuth2 authorization flows that hospital security teams have already approved
why: The practical blocker is the installed base: ancillary devices and systems that only speak v2 would each require vendor changes or an engine translating in front of them. FHIR can model orders, results, and encounters, so that claim is false. No certification rule forbids retiring a v2 interface, and SMART on FHIR is itself built on OAuth2.

q: A receiving system stores the entire PID-5 value 'Smith^John^A' in its single last-name column. Which parsing step is missing?
opts: Splitting on the repetition separator so each part becomes its own repeat of the field
Splitting on the subcomponent separator, which divides family name from given name
Splitting on the component separator so family, given, and middle name land in separate columns
Running the field through the escape-sequence decoder before reading it
why: The caret separates components inside one field, so PID-5 should be split into family, given, and middle name. The repetition separator (tilde) would separate two complete names, such as a legal name and an alias. The subcomponent separator (ampersand) subdivides a single component further. Escape decoding handles literal delimiter characters in data, which this value does not contain.

q: A patient portal must remove an appointment from a patient's upcoming list as soon as the clinic cancels it. Which message should the portal's interface listen for?
opts: SIU^S12, the new-appointment notification re-sent with the same appointment ID
ADT^A11, cancel admit, since the visit never started
ORM^O01, since appointments are orders placed with a department
SIU^S15, the appointment-cancellation notification
why: SIU^S15 is the scheduling cancellation event. S12 announces a new booking and is not a cancellation signal. A11 cancels an admission or visit in the ADT stream, which is a different object than a scheduled appointment. ORM carries clinical orders; scheduling events travel in SIU.

q: An employer name such as 'Smith & Sons' can be sent as-is in an HL7 v2 field, because only the pipe is ever treated as a delimiter.
opts: True
False
why: With the default encoding characters, the ampersand is the subcomponent separator, so an unescaped ampersand splits the value into subcomponents and corrupts the field even though the pipes are untouched. Literal delimiter characters must be sent as escape sequences, and the receiver must decode them. The message still looks structurally valid, which is why this bug usually surfaces only as subtly wrong data downstream.

q: If an engine returns AA the moment it receives an inbound message and only afterward fails to deliver it to a downstream system, that AA was not incorrect.
opts: True
False
why: The AA vouched only for the engine's own acceptance of the message. Whether the downstream system later received and filed it is a separate question that the sender's acknowledgment never covered. This is why teams monitor queues and destination errors rather than treating a stream of AA codes as proof of end-to-end delivery.

q: A new lab interface specification calls for OML^O21 lab orders, but the EHR's legacy feed only emits ORM^O01. Which statement describes the situation most accurately?
opts: OML is the later lab-specific order message with a different structure, so the engine must remap segments
OML carries results, so the lab would be sending it back to the EHR rather than receiving orders
Only the message type in the header differs, so relabeling every message is enough to satisfy the lab
OML drops order-control segments, so the existing order-control mappings can be discarded
why: Later HL7 v2 versions split the general ORM into category-specific order messages such as OML for laboratory. Both communicate orders, but the structure differs, so the engine needs a real mapping. Results travel in ORU, not in an order message. Relabeling alone would produce structurally wrong messages. Order-control information is still carried in OML, so those mappings remain relevant.

q: Which of these events would an interface analyst expect to see carried in ADT messages? (Choose three.)
opts: A patient is transferred to another nursing unit
A lab finalizes a hemoglobin result
Registration corrects a patient's phone number
The MPI merges two duplicate patient records
A new radiology appointment is booked
why: Transfers (A02), demographic updates (A08), and patient merges (A40) are all patient-administration events and travel in ADT. A finalized lab value is a result and belongs in ORU. A newly booked appointment is a scheduling event carried in SIU. The scheduling distractor is the near miss, since it also involves a patient and a date.

q: Which statements about HL7 v2 acknowledgments are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: In enhanced mode, a commit-level accept can come back before the application finishes processing
An AE tells the sender the receiving system never received the message at all
MSA echoes the original control ID so the sender can pair each reply with its message
A sender that gets no reply within its timeout can safely assume the message was processed
An AR means the receiver refused the message outright instead of evaluating it
why: Enhanced mode separates a fast transport-level commit accept from a later application acknowledgment. MSA echoes the control ID so replies can be matched, and AR is an outright refusal. AE means the message did arrive and was evaluated before an application error occurred, so it is not a non-delivery signal. Silence is a timeout, which leaves the outcome unknown rather than successful.

q: Two facilities in one network each send PID-3 with MRN 004512, but for different patients, and the receiving system treats them as one person. Which part of the identifier was ignored?
opts: The identifier type code, which labels the value as a medical record number
The assigning authority, which names the system that issued the number
The check digit, which is unique to each facility
The patient class, which differs by facility
why: A bare number is only unique within the system that issued it; the assigning authority component says which system that is, so the same digits from two facilities are different identifiers. Both numbers are MRNs, so the type code would be identical and cannot separate them. A check digit is computed from the number, not assigned per facility. Patient class describes the visit in PV1 and has nothing to do with identifier uniqueness.

q: A lab sent a final potassium result. An hour later a new ORU arrives for the same order with a different value and a result status of C on that observation. What should the receiving interface do?
opts: Append it as a second, independent final result next to the first
Apply it as a correction to the existing result and flag it as corrected
Discard it, since a final result can never change
Reject it with an AR because the order number was already used
why: A result status of C marks a correction that replaces a previously final value, so the interface should update the existing result and show it as corrected. Appending it would leave two conflicting final values for one analyte. Discarding it preserves a wrong value, which is a patient-safety problem. Reusing an order number is normal for results on the same order, so AR would be an incorrect rejection.

q: A PID-3 value of 12345^^^HOSP^MR~98765^^^CLINIC^MR carries two separate patient identifiers rather than one identifier with extra components.
opts: True
False
why: The tilde is the repetition separator, so the field holds two complete identifiers. The carets inside each one separate components such as the assigning authority and the identifier type. People often read the whole string as one identifier with many components, which would make a parser drop the second number.

q: A panel ORU has three OBX results. After the engine's transformer regroups segments by segment type, a hemolysis comment shows up under the wrong analyte. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The comment's source code no longer matches the status on the observation it describes
The service identifier on the order segment was changed during the transform
The comment's position no longer places it immediately after the result it describes
The set ID on the comment does not match the observation identifier
why: NTE has no key pointing at its parent; it belongs to whichever segment directly precedes it, so regrouping segments by type orphans each comment. The comment source field only says who wrote the note, and nothing compares it with a result status. Changing the order's service identifier would not move comments between analytes. The set ID only numbers comments in sequence and is not matched against observation identifiers.

q: After a merger, the new hospital's engine receives messages containing a ZCC segment the old lab invented for a cost-center code. What is the right handling?
opts: Map it to the NTE segment, since Z-segments are deprecated notes
Reject messages that contain it, since the standard forbids segments outside the base specification
Interpret it using the receiving vendor's own ZCC definition, since Z-segment names are standardized across vendors
Get the sender's definition and either map the field deliberately or drop it, since the standard gives Z-segments no meaning
why: Z-segments are reserved for local extensions, so their meaning exists only in the documentation of whoever created them. The sensible response is to obtain that definition and then map or drop the content on purpose. They are not deprecated notes, and NTE is a free-text segment with different semantics. The standard explicitly permits Z-segments, so rejecting them is wrong. Names are not coordinated between vendors, so another site's ZCC may mean something else entirely.

q: A monitor that alerts when the live MLLP connection drops will also detect a missing nightly HL7 batch file.
opts: True
False
why: A batch file travels as a scheduled file transfer, a separate path from the live socket. The MLLP connection can stay up and healthy while the job that creates or delivers the batch silently fails. Monitoring needs both a stalled-connection check and an expected-file-arrived check.

q: Which statements about HL7 v2 versions and extensions are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: A system built for 2.5.1 can often still read a 2.3 message, since later versions mostly add optional content
A Z-segment is safe to send to any partner without prior agreement because receivers interpret Z-segments uniformly
The version declared in MSH may be older than what either system could support
Raising the declared version number is risk-free because later versions never change field usage
why: Backward-compatible evolution lets a newer implementation read older messages, and many feeds still declare an old version because nobody wants to touch a stable interface. Z-segments have no shared meaning, so partners must agree on them first. Changing the declared version without testing is risky because receivers may branch on that value and later versions can alter optionality or usage.

q: A radiology system posts a procedure charge that must reach the hospital's billing system through the engine. Which message type should that interface carry?
opts: ORU^R01, since the charge follows the completed study
SIU^S12, since the charge is tied to a booked appointment
ORM^O01, since the procedure was originally ordered
DFT^P03, a detailed financial transaction
why: Charges and credits are financial transactions and travel in DFT. ORU carries the clinical result of the study, not its billing event. SIU announces scheduling changes. ORM is the order going to the department. Each distractor is related to the same procedure, but only DFT is the financial record.

q: A developer splits each segment on the pipe and treats array index 1 as field 1, including for MSH. The sending application name comes out one position off. What explains this?
opts: In MSH the separator character itself counts as field 1, so the split array is shifted by one
MSH is numbered from zero while every other segment is numbered from one
The encoding characters contain a pipe, which adds an extra empty field
The sending application is repeated in two adjacent MSH fields after a transform
why: MSH-1 is the field separator itself, so splitting on it never yields MSH-1 as an element, and every later MSH field sits one index earlier than the field number suggests. The encoding characters are the caret, tilde, backslash, and ampersand, with no pipe among them. MSH is not numbered differently from other segments, and nothing in the standard repeats the sending application. MSH is the one segment that needs this special case.

q: In an ORU, an NTE segment appears directly after the OBR and before the first OBX. What does that comment describe?
opts: The first OBX result that follows it in the message
Every OBX result carried in the message
The whole order described by that OBR
The patient identified in the PID segment
why: NTE attaches to the segment immediately before it, so a note placed right after the OBR is an order-level comment. A note that followed an OBX would instead describe that specific result. NTE does not look forward to a later segment, and it does not fan out to every result or to the patient.

q: After an ADT^A02 transfer, the dietary system keeps delivering trays to the patient's old room. Which mapping error is most likely?
opts: It reads the patient's PID home address instead of the visit segment
It reads the prior location instead of the assigned location
It reads the attending doctor field in place of the room
It ignores the event timestamp in EVN and uses the send time
why: A transfer message carries both where the patient was and where the patient is now in the visit segment; mapping the prior location field rather than the assigned location (PV1-3) reproduces exactly this symptom. A PID address is the patient's home address and would not look like a room. Reading the attending doctor would produce a name, not a stale room. Ignoring the EVN time could affect ordering of events but would not systematically select the old room.

q: A sender transmits many messages on one MLLP connection before any replies arrive. Which value lets it pair each acknowledgment with the message it answers?
opts: The acknowledgment code, since AA, AE, and AR differ per message
The original control ID, echoed back in the MSA segment
The order in which replies arrive, since replies are guaranteed to return in send order
The sending facility name in the reply's header, which is unique per message
why: MSA echoes the control ID of the message being acknowledged, which is the designed pairing key. The ack code only reports an outcome and many messages share the same code. Arrival order is not a safe key because a receiver may process messages in parallel or after retries. A facility name identifies a system, not a message.

q: An EHR sends VXU messages to a state registry whenever it needs to retrieve a patient's immunization history from that registry.
opts: True
False
why: VXU is an unsolicited update that pushes vaccination records to the registry. Retrieving history is a query and response exchange, typically a query-by-parameter message answered with a response message. Mixing up the direction is a common reason a registry integration gets built backwards.

q: Which statements about placer and filler order numbers in HL7 v2 order and result messages are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: The placer number is assigned by the system that places the order
The filler number is generated by the EHR at the moment the order is placed
The placer number is reissued each time a result for the order is amended
Both appear in the common order segment and usually repeat in the observation request segment
why: The ordering system assigns the placer number and the fulfilling system assigns the filler number, and both appear in ORC and typically also in OBR. The filler number comes from the lab, pharmacy, or imaging system, not from the EHR placing the order. The placer number identifies the order and stays stable across amended results, which is what lets a correction find the original.

q: A dictation system first sends a discharge summary as an unsigned draft and later the signed version. The EHR must display only the signed one, marked authenticated. Which part of the message should drive that status?
opts: The document header segment's completion status
The order status in the observation request segment
The event reason code in EVN
The visit indicator in PV1
why: MDM messages carry document metadata in the TXA segment, including the completion status that distinguishes a draft from an authenticated document. OBR status describes an order, not a document's signature state. EVN's reason code explains why an event occurred and PV1 describes the encounter, so neither says how final the note is.

q: When a delayed ADT discharge arrives with an event time from three days earlier, the receiving system should stamp the discharge with the header's transmission time, because that is the authoritative moment of the event.
opts: True
False
why: The event-occurred time in EVN (EVN-6) records when the discharge really happened, which can differ from when the message was sent. Using transmission time would backdate or forward-date the encounter incorrectly, affecting length of stay, billing, and bed history. Header time only says when the sender built the message.

q: A sender needs immediate confirmation that the engine has taken custody of an order, but the EHR's filing step takes up to a minute. Which acknowledgment design fits without tripping the sender's ACK timeout?
opts: Original mode, but the receiver holds its only reply until filing finishes
Enhanced mode: a prompt commit accept on receipt, then an application acknowledgment after filing
Original mode, with an AA returned before the message is written to any queue
No acknowledgments at all, with the sender polling the EHR database for the order
why: Enhanced mode is built for this split: a fast transport-level accept proves custody, and a later application acknowledgment reports the filing outcome. Holding a single original-mode reply for a minute invites sender timeouts and duplicate retries. Replying AA before the message is stored risks claiming custody the receiver does not yet have. Skipping acknowledgments removes the sender's delivery signal entirely.

q: A payer wants a clinical summary that stays exactly as authored and attested, even if the live chart changes later. Which FHIR approach fits?
opts: A searchset Bundle re-run on demand, so it always reflects the current chart
A document Bundle whose first entry is a Composition describing the content
A transaction Bundle, since it records exactly which changes were applied
A subscription notification that fires whenever the record is updated
why: A document Bundle is a fixed, point-in-time collection led by a Composition, meant to be preserved and attested as authored. A re-run searchset reflects whatever the chart holds today, which is the opposite of a stable summary. A transaction Bundle is a set of write operations, not a clinical document. A subscription notifies about changes and does not produce an attested snapshot.

q: An analyst maps a CBC workflow to FHIR: the physician's order, an individual hemoglobin value, and the finalized report that groups all the values. Which resource trio fits, in that order?
opts: ServiceRequest, Observation, DiagnosticReport
Observation, DiagnosticReport, ServiceRequest
ServiceRequest, DiagnosticReport, Observation
MedicationRequest, Observation, Composition
why: An order is a ServiceRequest, a single measured value is an Observation, and the report that groups values under one status and conclusion is a DiagnosticReport. The other trios reorder those roles or swap in resources from other domains: MedicationRequest is a prescription order and Composition structures a clinical document, so neither models a lab order or lab report.

q: A client POSTs a new Patient, the response times out, and its retry creates a duplicate. The client knows the patient's MRN. Which FHIR feature prevents duplicate creation on retry?
opts: Re-sending the POST inside a batch Bundle, which deduplicates entries with identical content
A conditional read using If-None-Match with the patient's MRN as the validator
Conditional create, using If-None-Exist with an identifier search so a match prevents creation
Appending _count=1 to the POST URL so the server stores only a single copy
why: Conditional create lets the client state a search criterion (here the identifier) and the server creates the resource only if nothing matches, which makes a retry safe. Batch Bundles do no content-based deduplication. If-None-Match is an ETag validator for reads and caching, not an identifier search. _count only affects how many results a search returns and is meaningless on a create.

q: A standalone SMART app has no EHR session. It needs the authorization server to prompt the user to choose which chart to open and return that selection with the token. Which scope requests this?
opts: launch, which carries the EHR's opaque context handle
openid fhirUser, which returns the signed-in user's identity
offline_access, which issues a refresh token
launch/patient, which requests a patient-selection context
why: In a standalone launch the app asks for launch/patient so the server establishes a patient context and returns it with the token. The plain launch scope is for EHR launch, where the EHR hands the app an opaque launch value. openid fhirUser asks for the user's identity, and offline_access asks for a refresh token; neither supplies a patient context.

q: In a US Core profile, an element is flagged Must Support but has a minimum cardinality of 0. What does that mean for an app consuming the data?
opts: The element is optional, so servers are free to ignore it entirely
Every instance must include it, filled with a placeholder value when empty
The element is deprecated, so apps should skip it when parsing
Servers must send it when they hold data, and apps must handle it, but it can be absent
why: Must Support means implementers must be able to populate and process the element, but with a minimum of 0 an instance can still lack it when the source has nothing to say. It is not ignorable, so treating it as ignorable understates it. Requiring a placeholder in every instance describes a mandatory element, which is a different thing. Must Support is not a deprecation flag.

q: A health IT vendor's contract bars customer apps from reading data through its FHIR API unless they pay a steep per-call fee, 'for security.' Which federal rule is the most likely compliance concern?
opts: The information-blocking provisions that restrict interference with access to health information
The HIPAA Security Rule's addressable specification for encryption at rest
The special consent requirements for substance use disorder treatment records
The voluntary common agreement between qualified health information networks
why: Practices that unreasonably restrict access, exchange, or use of electronic health information, including prohibitive fees, fall under the information-blocking rules, which are also a main reason vendors expose usable FHIR APIs. The encryption specification concerns stored data safeguards. The Part 2 consent rules govern a specific category of records. The common agreement for networks is a voluntary framework, not a rule about vendor fees.

q: A vendor needs unattended nightly extracts for many patients, while a consumer app needs one patient's data after that patient signs in. Which pairing of approaches fits?
opts: Patient-facing launch for the vendor, and backend services authorization for the consumer app
Backend services authorization for both, since patient sign-in only adds friction
EHR launch with user scopes for both, since both are tied to a clinician login
Backend services with system scopes for the vendor, and patient-facing launch with patient scopes for the app
why: Unattended, population-level access has no user to sign in, so it uses backend services authorization and system scopes. An app acting for a patient needs that patient to authenticate and be bound to their own data with patient scopes. Swapping the two gives a batch job an interactive login or a consumer app unbounded access. Neither integration involves a clinician's EHR session.

q: A payer kicks off a Bulk FHIR export for a group and gets HTTP 202 with a status URL in a response header and no data. What should it do next?
opts: Poll the status URL until the export completes, then download the files its manifest lists
Treat 202 as a failure and resend the kickoff request until it returns 200 with data
Parse the 202 body as a Bundle of the group's patients
Register a Subscription on the group so the server pushes the files when ready
why: Bulk export is asynchronous: the 202 acknowledges the job, and the client polls the status URL until it returns the completion manifest with links to the newline-delimited JSON files. Resending the kickoff would start duplicate jobs. The 202 response carries no patient Bundle. Bulk export defines polling, not a Subscription push, for delivery.

q: A Patient resource's logical id on a FHIR server is the same value as the patient's MRN, so another system can look the patient up by that id.
opts: True
False
why: The logical id is assigned by the server and is only meaningful there. The MRN belongs in the identifier element, with a system URL saying who issued it, and other systems should search by identifier. Treating the logical id as a business identifier breaks as soon as data moves to a second server.

q: A 403 response to a request carrying a valid, unexpired access token usually means the token's granted scopes do not cover the request, whereas an expired token would normally produce a 401.
opts: True
False
why: A 401 signals that authentication failed, for example a missing, invalid, or expired token. A 403 means the server knew who the caller was and refused the action, which in SMART on FHIR usually points to scopes that do not include the resource type or operation. Telling the two apart tells you whether to refresh the token or change the requested scopes.

q: A server whose Patient endpoint conforms to the US Core Patient profile has therefore demonstrated support for every USCDI data class.
opts: True
False
why: USCDI spans many data classes, such as problems, medications, allergies, labs, and immunizations, and each is covered by its own US Core profiles. Conformance on Patient shows only that one resource type meets its profile. Claiming USCDI support requires the other classes too.

q: Which pairings of clinical concept and FHIR resource are correct? (Choose three.)
opts: A prescription is a MedicationRequest; what the patient reports taking is a MedicationStatement
A diagnosis on the problem list is an Observation carrying a diagnosis code
A patient's insurance plan membership is represented by a Coverage resource
A clinician's bookable availability is modeled as an Encounter resource
A signed discharge summary is typically a DocumentReference or Composition
why: MedicationRequest versus MedicationStatement, Coverage for insurance membership, and DocumentReference or Composition for clinical documents are all correct. A problem-list diagnosis is a Condition, not an Observation, even though both can carry codes. Availability is modeled by Schedule and Slot; an Encounter describes an interaction that actually occurs.

q: Which statements about SMART on FHIR scopes and launch are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: Patient scopes confine an app to one patient; user scopes follow the signed-in user's access
An EHR launch hands the app a launch value that it returns in its authorization request
Backend services use system scopes because no user is present
The granted scopes always equal the scopes requested, because servers cannot narrow them
A standalone app can never receive a patient context from the authorization server
why: Patient versus user scope prefixes, the launch value in EHR launch, and system scopes for unattended backend services are all accurate. Authorization servers and users can grant less than the app requested, so apps must read the granted scope from the token response. A standalone app can obtain a patient context by requesting a launch scope that triggers patient selection.

q: A client must find out whether a server honors a particular Observation search parameter before building a feature on it. Which approach is reliable?
opts: Run a test search with the parameter and treat HTTP 200 as proof the server honors it
Read the Observation StructureDefinition, which lists every parameter the server accepts
Fetch the server's CapabilityStatement from its metadata endpoint and read the Observation search parameters it declares
Read the base specification for the server's FHIR version, since all servers implement every parameter
why: The CapabilityStatement is where a server declares what it supports, including search parameters per resource type. A 200 proves little because servers commonly ignore parameters they do not recognize and return unfiltered results unless the client requests strict handling. A StructureDefinition describes the resource's shape, not this server's search support. The specification defines what exists, not what a given server implements.

q: A report built on a FHIR search for Observations always shows exactly 50 rows although thousands match, and no error is logged. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The request lacked _include, so the server withheld the remaining matches
The client read the first page of the searchset Bundle and never followed its next link
The patient compartment caps any result set at 50 resources
The search was wrapped in a batch Bundle, which processes at most 50 entries
why: Servers page large result sets, and the client is expected to follow the Bundle's next link until none remains. A silent page limit produces exactly this under-reporting. _include only pulls in referenced resources and does not restrict how many matches return. Compartments define scope, not a result cap, and batch Bundles have no 50-entry limit.

q: A client sends a version-aware update with an If-Match header holding the version it read, and the server rejects it as a precondition failure. What most likely happened?
opts: The token's scopes do not allow updates to that resource type
The resource was deleted, so there is nothing to update
Another client changed the resource after this client read it
The resource violated a profile's required terminology binding
why: If-Match with a version protects against lost updates: if the stored version no longer matches what the client read, the server refuses and the client must re-read and merge. Scope problems are authorization failures, a deleted resource is reported as gone, and a profile violation is a validation failure, so none of those is a precondition mismatch.

q: Which statements about FHIR search are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: Results may be paged, so a client may need to follow the Bundle's next link
An identifier search can pair a system with a value to match one issuer's numbers
_include adds the resources referenced by the matches to the same searchset Bundle
_revinclude adds the resources that the matches themselves reference
A request containing an unrecognized parameter always fails with an error from the server
why: Paging, system-qualified identifier searches, and _include for referenced resources are all accurate. _revinclude works in the opposite direction: it adds resources that refer to the matches, such as Observations pointing at the Patients found. By default servers may ignore unrecognized parameters rather than fail, which is why a test search is not proof of support.

q: An engine copies Observations from one FHIR server to another, leaving subject.reference as 'Patient/123'. On the target, some Observations point at the wrong patient or at nothing. Why?
opts: Reference elements can only hold display names, so the engine truncated the id portion
FHIR forbids references from crossing between servers, so the target dropped them
Relative references and ids are server-specific, so the engine must remap them or use identifiers
The engine should have embedded each Patient as a contained resource inside every Observation
why: A relative reference like Patient/123 only has meaning on the server that issued that id, so after a copy it may resolve to a different patient or none. The engine must translate ids, use absolute references, or match by business identifier. References hold ids or URLs, not names. FHIR does not forbid cross-server references, and contained resources are a narrow convenience that would not make Patient data shared or reusable.

q: A clinic wants Patient resources, and only Patients, who have an Observation with a particular LOINC code. Which search feature filters Patients by a property of the Observations that reference them?
opts: Forward chaining on subject.name from the Observation endpoint
Reverse chaining with _has on the Patient search
_include on a Patient search
_revinclude on a Patient search
why: _has is reverse chaining: it keeps Patients for which a referencing Observation matches the stated criteria. Forward chaining from the Observation endpoint returns Observations, not Patients. _include and _revinclude do not filter the primary results at all; they only attach additional resources to whichever Patients the search already returned.

q: A client must create a new Patient and an Encounter that references it in one request, before the server has assigned any ids. Which approach works?
opts: A batch Bundle with the same references, since batch entries can see each other's new ids
A searchset Bundle holding both entries, which the server stores when it receives it
A transaction Bundle in which the Encounter refers to the Patient entry's temporary urn:uuid id
A document Bundle, which commits both resources once the Composition is signed
why: A transaction Bundle lets entries refer to each other by temporary identifiers, and the server resolves them to real ids as it processes the unit atomically. Batch entries are independent and cannot depend on one another's assigned ids. A searchset is a response container, not a way to submit creates. A document Bundle is a fixed clinical document, not an instruction to persist resources.

q: A receiver that does not recognize an ordinary extension may safely ignore it, but it must not ignore a modifier extension it does not understand.
opts: True
False
why: Ordinary extensions add information without changing the meaning of the rest of the resource, so ignoring an unknown one is safe. A modifier extension can change how the whole element or resource must be interpreted, such as negating a statement, so a receiver that cannot process it should not treat the resource as understood. The distinction matters whenever partners exchange custom data.

q: Which statements about transaction and batch Bundles are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: If one entry in a transaction fails, none of its changes are persisted
A batch response reports a separate status for each entry
Entries in a batch may rely on each other's newly assigned ids
A transaction always executes entries in the order they are listed
A searchset Bundle is a server response, not operations a client submits
why: Atomicity for transactions, per-entry results for batches, and searchset as a response container are all accurate. Batch entries are processed independently and cannot depend on one another. Servers process transaction entries in a defined order by operation type, with deletes before creates before updates before reads, rather than strictly in the order listed, so order-dependent logic should not assume list order.

q: A vitals Observation must be tied to the specific hospital stay in which it was taken, not just to the patient. Which element does that?
opts: Observation.subject, holding a reference to the Encounter
Observation.encounter, holding a reference to the Encounter
Observation.performer, holding a reference to the Location of the stay
Observation.basedOn, holding a reference to the Encounter
why: Observation.encounter exists specifically to link a measurement to the visit during which it was made. Observation.subject identifies who or what the observation is about, typically the Patient. Performer names who carried it out, and basedOn points at the request that prompted it, such as a ServiceRequest; neither is where the stay is recorded.

q: An app holds a valid token with the scope patient/Observation.read for patient 123 and requests Observations for patient 456. What should a compliant server do?
opts: Return them, since scopes limit resource types and not whose data is read
Deny the request, since the token is bound to the patient in context
Return them with identifiers removed so the data is de-identified
Return only the Observations not marked sensitive
why: A patient-level scope confines the token to the patient in context, so a request for a different patient must be refused. Scopes constrain both the resource type and whose data it covers, so returning them misreads the scope. Stripping identifiers is not a de-identification method a server applies on the fly, and filtering sensitive items would still leak another patient's data.

q: A client submits a batch Bundle of five independent create entries, and the third fails validation. What does the client get back?
opts: A failure for the whole Bundle, with none of the five entries persisted on the server
A separate status per entry: four created and one failed with an OperationOutcome
A response containing only the failing entry, since the others are assumed fine
Four created entries held as drafts until the third entry is fixed and resubmitted
why: Batch entries are independent, so the server returns a batch-response with one result per entry: four successes and one failure with details. All-or-nothing behavior belongs to transaction Bundles. Servers do not omit successful entries from the response, and FHIR has no draft state that holds creates until a sibling entry is fixed.

q: An engine maps a hospital's local code for serum potassium to a standard so partners can compare results. Which code system does US Core expect for identifying the lab test in Observation.code?
opts: ICD-10-CM
LOINC
CPT
SNOMED CT
why: LOINC identifies laboratory tests and is the system expected for lab Observation codes. ICD-10-CM classifies diagnoses and CPT classifies billable procedures, so neither names the test. SNOMED CT is a broad clinical terminology that appears elsewhere, for example for problems or qualitative results, which is why it is the tempting near miss.

q: A pathology lab sends a signed PDF report plus structured findings. Which DiagnosticReport elements carry the PDF and the structured findings?
opts: result for the PDF, presentedForm for the Observations
presentedForm for the PDF, result for the Observations
conclusion for the PDF, basedOn for the Observations
Composition.section for both
why: presentedForm holds the report as an attachment such as a PDF, while result references the Observation resources with the structured values. The swapped pairing reverses those roles. conclusion is a text summary and basedOn references the originating request, and Composition.section belongs to a different resource used for documents.

q: A care-coordination app needs one patient's full record in a single call, while a nightly job needs 200,000 patients. Which operations match?
opts: Bulk $export for the app, and $everything for the nightly job
$everything for both, looping over each patient in the job
$everything for the app, and Bulk $export for the nightly job
Bulk $export for both, with the app discarding other patients' files
why: $everything on a Patient returns one patient's clinically relevant resources in a single Bundle, suited to a chart-summary app. Bulk export is asynchronous and designed for population-scale extracts. Looping $everything for 200,000 patients wastes calls the bulk operation avoids. Using bulk for one patient's interactive view is slow and exposes other patients' data to an app that should never see it.

q: A team designs a v2-to-FHIR mapping for an ADT^A01 admit. Which pairings are sensible? (Choose three.)
opts: PID demographics map to a Patient resource
The EVN segment maps to an AllergyIntolerance resource
PV1 visit details map to an Encounter resource
The PV1 attending doctor maps to a Coverage resource
MSH routing metadata maps to a MessageHeader in a message-style Bundle
why: Patient demographics, visit details, and header metadata map naturally to Patient, Encounter, and MessageHeader. EVN carries event type and timing, which has nothing to do with allergies. An attending doctor is a Practitioner referenced from the Encounter, not an insurance Coverage.

q: Which statements about clinical terminologies are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: RxNorm gives normalized names for clinical drugs independent of package
NDC identifies a specific packaged drug product
ICD-10-CM is the standard way to identify which laboratory test was performed
UCUM expresses units of measure on numeric results
CPT codes the diagnoses on a patient's problem list
why: RxNorm names the clinical drug, NDC identifies the actual packaged product, and UCUM standardizes units such as mg/dL. ICD-10-CM classifies diagnoses, and lab tests are identified with LOINC. CPT is a procedure coding system used for billing, not the vocabulary for problem-list diagnoses.

q: A compliance officer wants to answer two questions: who authored this Condition and from which system, and who has viewed this chart. Which resource pairing fits?
opts: AuditEvent for both questions, since it logs every event touching a resource
Provenance for both questions, since it tracks everything about a resource
Provenance for the first question and AuditEvent for the second
Consent for the first question and OperationOutcome for the second
why: Provenance records who created or changed a resource and where it came from, while AuditEvent records access and activity such as who viewed it. Using one resource for both blurs authorship with access logging. Consent records a patient's permissions and OperationOutcome reports the result of an operation, so neither answers either question.

q: Once a FHIR Consent resource is recorded for a patient, the server automatically blocks any request for the covered data that the consent does not permit.
opts: True
False
why: Consent is a structured record of a patient's permissions or refusals. It does not enforce itself. Enforcement lives in the access-control or authorization layer, which must read the consent and apply it, which is why a stored Consent that nobody consults protects nothing.

q: Which statements about OperationOutcome, AuditEvent, and Provenance are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: A server may attach an OperationOutcome to a successful response to carry warnings
OperationOutcome issues carry a severity such as fatal, error, warning, or information
An OperationOutcome is valid only in responses to failed requests
AuditEvent can record both successful and failed access attempts
Provenance is the resource intended for logging who read a chart
why: OperationOutcome can accompany success to report warnings, has severity levels, and AuditEvent records access outcomes of both kinds. OperationOutcome is not limited to failures. Provenance describes the origin and authorship of a resource rather than who read it, which is the job of AuditEvent.

q: A client POSTs well-formed JSON for an Observation, but its code violates a required terminology binding in the server's profile. Which response is most appropriate?
opts: 400 Bad Request with an OperationOutcome saying the JSON cannot be parsed
422 Unprocessable Entity with an OperationOutcome naming the violated binding
201 Created, with the profile problem flagged for later cleanup
404 Not Found, because the server cannot locate the profile
why: A resource that parses correctly but breaks a profile or server business rule is reported as 422 with an OperationOutcome explaining what is wrong. 400 is for a request that cannot be parsed or fails basic validation, which does not describe well-formed JSON. Creating the resource anyway defeats the purpose of the profile, and 404 refers to a missing resource, not a rule violation.

q: A manager suggests treating the engine's message archive as the legal record of lab results because it holds every ORU. What is the strongest objection?
opts: Engines cannot store message content at all, only the acknowledgments they return
It is a pruned troubleshooting aid, while the EHR has amendment and retention controls
Transformed messages are encrypted in the archive, so nobody can read them later
The archive holds only the first message per order, so later corrections are lost
why: Integration engines are middleware: they keep copies for troubleshooting and replay, typically pruned on a schedule, but they lack the clinical record-keeping controls of the EHR such as amendments, attestations, and retention rules. Engines can and do store message content. Archives are not generally encrypted into unreadability, and they keep every message rather than only the first per order.

q: The EHR team calls the order feed to the lab 'outbound,' while the lab's team calls the same feed 'inbound.' Who is correct?
opts: Only the EHR team, since the EHR is the system of record and defines direction
Whichever system is named first in the engine channel's name, by convention
Both, since direction depends on which side is describing it, so specs should name the system
Neither, since the label depends on whether the transport is MLLP or a file
why: The same connection is outbound for the sender and inbound for the receiver, so both labels are right from their own side. Specifications should say 'outbound from the EHR' rather than just 'outbound'. Being the system of record does not change direction, channel naming is a convention rather than a rule, and transport type has no bearing on direction.

q: In generic, publicly discussed terms, which Epic components handle a SMART app's FHIR access and an overnight HL7 v2 lab feed?
opts: Bridges for the app's FHIR access, Interconnect for the lab feed
Interconnect for the app's FHIR access, Bridges for the lab feed
Bridges for both, since it is the only interface component
Interconnect for both, since it replaced HL7 v2 traffic handling
why: In public descriptions, Interconnect is the web-services and API layer that exposes FHIR to external apps, while Bridges handles HL7 v2 message traffic with external systems such as labs. The swapped pairing reverses those roles. Neither component handles both kinds of traffic, and Interconnect does not replace v2 message handling.

q: An engine's ADT channel receives normally and its other destinations are current, but one destination's queue keeps growing and its ACK latency climbs. Where should troubleshooting start?
opts: The source connector, since inbound traffic is what fills queues
The engine host's CPU, since a failing engine would delay a single destination while the others stay current
The slow destination system or the connection to it, since messages pile up at the last healthy point
The channel filter, which holds messages until a rule passes
why: A backlog at one destination with healthy peers points at that destination or its link: messages accumulate where delivery slows. Normal inbound traffic and current sibling destinations argue against a source problem. An engine-wide fault would slow every destination, not one. Filters accept or reject a message and do not hold it waiting for a rule.

q: After a lab vendor upgrade, a downstream parser starts failing on ORU messages and ACKs come back as AE, though volume is normal. What should you do first?
opts: Restart the channel to clear any stale parser state left over from the upgrade
Diff a failing message against a known-good one and the specification to find what changed
Replay all failed messages immediately to see whether they pass on a second attempt
Raise the ACK timeout so the parser has longer to finish processing each message
why: Normal volume with application errors right after an upgrade suggests a changed message structure, so diffing a failing message against a good one and the specification pinpoints the change before anything is altered. Restarting does not fix a deterministic parsing difference. Replaying failures just regenerates the same errors, and a longer timeout addresses missing replies, but here replies are arriving.

q: A mapping change passed every test the analyst wrote but broke on the first live message with a blank PV1 location. What testing gap does this show?
opts: The test set did not reflect real traffic variation, such as blank or missing fields
The change should have been tested directly in production before any other environment
Non-production environments cannot parse HL7 v2 messages reliably enough to test
Testing is unnecessary on any interface that already has a documented rollback plan
why: Hand-written samples tend to be tidy, so a representative test set drawn from real traffic patterns (with PHI protections) is needed to cover blanks, repeats, and odd values. Testing in production is the practice the process exists to avoid. Non-production engines parse v2 fine. A rollback plan limits damage but does not replace testing.

q: With a hub-and-spoke engine, a sending system's format change can often be absorbed by updating that system's own channel mapping rather than editing every partner's interface.
opts: True
False
why: Because each system connects only to the hub, the translation to each partner lives in the engine. A sender's change can often be handled by adjusting one mapping while partners continue to receive the format they expect. In a point-to-point mesh, every partner connection would have to be changed separately.

q: A queue depth of zero on every channel proves that all interfaces are healthy.
opts: True
False
why: An empty queue can also mean nothing is arriving, for example when a sender has stopped or a connection has silently died. Queue depth has to be read alongside message volume against a baseline, and a canary message confirms end-to-end delivery.

q: A source connection shows 'connected' but inbound volume has dropped to zero, with no errors logged. Which causes are consistent with that? (Choose three.)
opts: The sending system's export job stopped
A firewall dropped the session after an idle timeout, leaving a half-open connection
The sender is holding messages in its own outbound queue after a fault
A schema mismatch at the receiving parser rejecting each incoming message
A steady stream of AE acknowledgments returned from a destination system
why: A stopped export, a half-open connection, and a backed-up sender queue all produce silence with a connection that still looks up. A schema mismatch and AE acknowledgments would both generate errors and visible traffic rather than silence, so they do not fit the symptoms.

q: Which tasks belong in a channel's filter rather than its transformer? (Choose three.)
opts: Accepting only ADT messages from one facility
Converting local sex codes to standard values
Dropping messages for test patients before they go further
Restructuring segments to match the destination's layout
Stopping messages whose type is anything other than ORU^R01
why: Filters make accept-or-reject decisions about whether a message continues. Facility restrictions, test-patient exclusion, and message-type gating are all such decisions. Converting coded values and restructuring segments reshape a message that was already accepted, which is the transformer's job.

q: An engine converts v2 ADT messages to FHIR Patient resources. The v2 carries a site-specific cost-center code in a Z-segment with no FHIR equivalent. Which handling is most defensible?
opts: Place it in Patient.name.text so it travels along with the demographic record
Let the engine drop unmapped content silently so that conversions never fail
Reject every message that contains a Z-segment until the sender removes it
Carry it as a mutually agreed extension, or omit it deliberately and document the gap
why: Locally defined data has no standard home, so either both sides agree on an extension definition or the field is dropped knowingly and documented. Hiding it in the name text corrupts a demographic field. Silent dropping hides data loss, and rejecting messages with Z-segments would stop legitimate feeds.

q: A destination is down for 20 minutes. Its queue now holds an admit, a demographic update, and a discharge for one patient, which must be applied in event order. Which queue behavior fits?
opts: Drain in order for that patient, accepting slower recovery than parallel delivery
Drain with many parallel threads for speed, since each message carries a timestamp
Drain newest-first so the latest status wins
Send only the last message per patient, since earlier ones are obsolete
why: ADT events build on each other, so order must be preserved for a patient even though that limits throughput. Parallel threads can apply a discharge before the admit it depends on. Newest-first reverses history, and sending only the last message would hand the destination a discharge for a patient it never saw admitted.

q: Which error-handling behaviors are appropriate for a production channel? (Choose three.)
opts: Retrying transient failures such as a refused connection, with a delay between attempts
Sending data-validation failures to an error queue for review instead of retrying forever
Retrying validation failures indefinitely, since the destination might accept them later
Alerting when messages are sitting in the error queue
Deleting failed messages after the retry limit to keep queues short
why: Transient failures deserve delayed retries, deterministic failures belong in an error queue, and an unwatched error queue helps no one, so alerting matters. Retrying a validation failure forever wastes resources and blocks the queue. Deleting failed messages silently loses clinical data.

q: An engine maps a lab's local code K+ to a standard LOINC code. Months later the lab quietly changes what K+ means, yet the mapping runs without a single error. What does this show?
opts: The transformer has a syntax defect that should have failed deployment testing
The filter should have rejected any message whose code had changed meaning
LOINC codes are unstable and must be re-mapped from scratch each quarter
A valid mapping can turn clinically wrong, so tables need an owner told of source changes
why: Mapping logic encodes assumptions about the source, and nothing in the engine can detect a change of meaning that leaves the format intact. The control is organizational: an owner of the mapping table who is notified when the source changes. The transformer is syntactically fine, a filter cannot know a code's meaning shifted, and LOINC is stable by design.

q: A destination rejects the same ADT message with AR for an unsupported message version, and five retries return the same result. What should the engine do?
opts: Keep retrying with longer delays until the destination eventually accepts it
Discard it silently, since an AR is the receiver's last word on the matter
Move it to a dead-letter queue and alert, since retrying cannot fix a repeatable rejection
Convert the AR to AA so the sender stops retrying and clears its queue
why: A repeatable rejection will not change with more attempts, so the message is set aside for a person to fix the underlying version issue and reprocess. Endless retries burn resources, and silent discard loses data. Rewriting AR as AA falsifies the delivery status and hides a real failure from the sender.

q: Running the hub of a hub-and-spoke network as a cluster removes the single point of failure for a downstream system that is itself offline.
opts: True
False
why: Clustering keeps the engine available if a node fails, but it does nothing for a destination system that is down. That case is covered by store-and-forward queuing, retry policies, and alerting. Confusing the two leaves downstream outages unplanned for.

q: Which alerts would catch a silently failed feed? (Choose three.)
opts: Volume for a feed falling below its time-of-day baseline
Alerting only on messages that reach an ERROR status in the engine log
A canary message that fails to reach its destination end to end
The age of the oldest queued message exceeding a threshold
Engine host CPU rising above 80 percent for more than five minutes
why: A silent failure produces no errors, so detection depends on baselines, end-to-end probes, and queue age. An error-only alert misses it by definition, and CPU load says little about whether a specific feed is flowing.

q: A sender hits an ACK timeout and retries three times. The pharmacy system, which had processed the original, now holds four identical orders. What control was missing?
opts: A longer ACK timeout, which removes the need for any retries at all
A filter on the sending system's name in the message header
An AE response generated by the receiver on every retry attempt
Duplicate detection on the control ID, so repeats are recognized and ignored
why: A timeout does not mean the message failed; the original may have arrived and only the reply was lost. Idempotent handling that recognizes a repeated control ID turns a retry into a harmless no-op. A longer timeout merely delays the same ambiguity, a sender-name filter cannot tell a repeat from a new message, and AE responses would convert retries into errors rather than prevent duplicates.

q: Two teams disagree on whether a field is required in a new interface. Which source should settle it?
opts: The base HL7 v2 standard, which defines exactly what each site must populate
The latest sample message the vendor sent, since it shows real usage
Whatever the production engine currently accepts without error
The jointly agreed interface specification, since base HL7 v2 leaves most fields optional
why: Because HL7 v2 leaves so much optional, the contract between two systems is the interface specification both teams agreed to. The base standard cannot settle site-level requirements, one sample message may omit fields that are normally present, and what an engine currently tolerates reflects its leniency, not the agreement.

q: A message sent to a channel with three destinations reaches two of them but never the third, and the source connector shows no error. Where should you look first?
opts: The source connector's listener port and its connection settings
The source-level filter, which rejects messages for only one destination
The sender's application name in the message header
The third destination's own filter, transformer, or connection settings
why: Two destinations succeeded, so the source accepted and processed the message; the divergence lies in what is specific to the third destination. A listener port problem would block all messages, and a source-level filter applies to every destination equally. The sender's header value is the same for all three routes.

q: An engine receives one ADT feed carrying every facility. Only Facility B's admissions should reach Facility B's bed-management system. What routing must the engine use?
opts: Type-based routing on ADT, since all admissions share one message type
Store-and-forward queuing, since it holds messages for the right destination
Content-based routing on the facility value in the message
Hub-and-spoke routing, since the hub knows each spoke's facility
why: Choosing a destination by a value inside the message is content-based routing. Type-based routing would send every ADT message to Facility B regardless of origin. Store-and-forward is a reliability pattern, and hub-and-spoke is a topology; neither inspects message contents to pick a destination.

q: If ten systems all exchange data with one another, point-to-point wiring needs up to 45 connections, while a hub-and-spoke design needs ten.
opts: True
False
why: Ten systems pairwise give 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 possible connections, whereas each system connecting once to a central engine gives ten. The gap widens quickly as systems are added, which is why hospitals migrate from meshes to hubs.

q: Which designs make a retry safe? (Choose three.)
opts: Deduplicating on the sender's message control ID
Keying orders on the placer order number so a repeat updates the existing order
A FHIR conditional create with If-None-Exist, for resources that carry an identifier
Deduplicating on message timestamps alone, without any other identifier
Lowering the ACK timeout so that retries happen much faster
why: A control ID, a stable business key, and a conditional create each let the receiver recognize a repeat. Timestamps alone are a poor key because distinct messages can share a time and a retry may be stamped differently. A shorter timeout produces more retries, not safer ones.

q: A hospital is migrating its interfaces from one commercial engine to another. Which work product carries over best?
opts: Exported channel configuration files, which import across commercial engines unchanged
Interface specifications and mapping rules, rebuilt in the new tool's own language
Stored routing queues, which the new engine simply adopts as they stand
The hub-and-spoke topology, which must be redesigned for the new vendor's product
why: The documented logic, meaning specifications and mapping rules, is portable even though it must be re-implemented in a different tool. Products use proprietary configuration formats, so exports do not import unchanged. Queues belong to the running engine and are drained or replayed rather than adopted, and the hub-and-spoke architecture itself carries over rather than needing redesign.

q: A hospital's engine runs as a two-node cluster, yet when the pharmacy system goes offline for three hours, pharmacy-bound messages still pile up. Why didn't clustering help?
opts: Clustering protects the engine's own availability, not a destination's, so queuing and alerting cover that case
A cluster fails over only when the sending system pauses transmission, which did not happen
Standby nodes keep configuration only, so queued messages cannot be shared across nodes
Clusters duplicate each message to both nodes, which doubles the backlog but not the delay
why: Clustering addresses failure of the engine itself. A downstream outage still stops delivery, which is why store-and-forward queuing and alerts are needed. Failover is triggered by node failure, not by sender behavior. Cluster nodes commonly share queue state, and duplicating messages across nodes is not what clustering does.

q: A message rejected by a channel filter is automatically sent to the dead-letter queue for review.
opts: True
False
why: A filter rejection is a deliberate accept-or-reject decision, so the message is simply recorded as filtered and goes no further. Dead-letter queues hold messages that failed delivery or processing after retries. Treating filtered messages as failures would flood the review queue, and treating failures as filtered ones would hide them.

q: Which situations are better served by asynchronous messaging than by a synchronous call? (Choose three.)
opts: An ADT update broadcast to eight downstream systems, where the sender must not wait on any of them
A real-time eligibility check the front desk needs answered before continuing
A nightly charge file posted to the billing system
A decision-support check shown to a clinician before an order is signed
A lab result notification pushed to a portal when the report is finalized
why: Broadcasts, nightly postings, and event notifications do not need an immediate answer, so asynchronous delivery suits them. An eligibility check and a pre-signing decision-support check both hold up a person's workflow until a response arrives, so they need a synchronous request and response.

q: A downstream system handles 20 messages per second, but a mass registration sends 200 per second for ten minutes. Which approach protects the downstream system without losing messages?
opts: Discard messages above the rate limit and rely on the sender to resend them later
Forward at full speed and let the downstream system's own queue absorb the surge
Throttle the delivery rate and queue the excess, accepting some delay
Switch the destination to fire-and-forget so it no longer needs to keep up
why: Throttling paces delivery to what the destination can take while queued messages wait their turn, trading delay for safety. Discarding relies on a resend that may never come. Forwarding at full speed risks overwhelming the system, and fire-and-forget only removes the engine's visibility into the problem.

q: Replaying a backlog of old dead-lettered ADT messages can overwrite newer patient data, so ordering and currency must be considered before reprocessing.
opts: True
False
why: After a fix, replayed messages describe the past: an old demographic update could replace a newer correction, or a stale location could reappear. Teams confirm the root cause is fixed, check how current each message is, and replay in a controlled order.

q: A hospital already has its EHR vendor's built-in HL7 interface component. Which situation most justifies also deploying a separate commercial engine?
opts: Many non-EHR devices and systems need to exchange data with each other, not via the EHR
The EHR vendor's built-in component cannot send any outbound messages at all
Regulation requires each hospital to run two engines for the sake of redundancy
A separate engine removes the need for a master patient index entirely
why: An EHR's interface component is built around the EHR, so traffic among ancillary systems that never touch the EHR is a natural case for a general-purpose engine. The EHR's component can send outbound messages, no regulation mandates two engines, and an engine does not replace patient identity matching.

q: An MPI links two records only when first name, last name, and date of birth match exactly. 'Jon' and 'John' Smith, same birthday and address, stay unlinked. What is this failure, and what approach reduces it?
opts: A fragmented history; weighted matching across several fields reduces it
An overlay error; stricter exact matching reduces it
A fragmented history; requiring even more exact-match fields reduces it
An overlay error; weighted matching across several fields removes it
why: One real person split across unlinked records is a fragmented history, and tolerant weighted matching, which scores partial agreement on several fields, can link 'Jon' and 'John' when everything else agrees. Overlay is the opposite failure, two people merged. Requiring more exact fields makes missed matches more likely, and weighted matching can itself produce overlays if thresholds are loose, so it does not remove them.

q: A matching run merged two different patients into one chart, and a nurse has already documented medications on it. What should happen first?
opts: Wait for the next nightly matching run to correct the merge on its own
Delete the older record so a single clean chart remains for the patient
Alert clinical staff and flag the chart, then unmerge through the controlled process
Raise the matching threshold and leave the existing link in place for now
why: An overlay is a live patient-safety hazard, so the first step is to stop clinicians from relying on the combined chart and then separate the records through a controlled unmerge. Waiting a night leaves wrong data in use. Deleting a record destroys legitimate clinical history. Changing the threshold prevents future merges but does nothing about this one.

q: An engine connects to a lab over TLS but writes full HL7 messages to a log file that every analyst can read. Which risk does TLS leave open?
opts: Interception of messages on the network between the engine and the lab
Exposure of PHI at rest and to people with no need to see it
Replay of a message after an ACK timeout
A schema mismatch between sender and receiver
why: TLS protects data in transit, so network interception is the risk it already covers. Unencrypted logs readable by everyone are a separate at-rest and minimum-necessary problem that TLS cannot touch. Replay after a timeout is an idempotency concern, and a schema mismatch is a data-format failure; neither is a confidentiality exposure created here.

q: A production results interface is down and clinicians cannot see labs. A tested fix exists, but the next scheduled window is two days away. What is most appropriate?
opts: Wait for the scheduled window regardless of the effect on patient care
Use the emergency change process: approval, notice, rollback plan, documentation, then deploy
Apply the fix directly, since an emergency bypasses change control altogether
Apply it in the test environment and assume production will follow suit
why: Emergencies call for an expedited, not absent, change process: someone with authority approves, affected teams are told, a rollback plan exists, and the change is documented. Waiting two days ignores real patient impact. Bypassing control removes the safeguards that protect the interface, and a test-environment change does not repair production.

q: A clinician at one hospital queries an outside hospital's records for an emergency department patient through a cross-organization exchange. What generally permits this under HIPAA without a new patient signature?
opts: A signed Business Associate Agreement between the two hospitals
Safe Harbor de-identification of the records before they leave the outside hospital
Treatment disclosures are permitted without patient authorization
Specific opt-in consent for every individual disclosure
why: Disclosures for treatment are permitted without patient authorization, which is why exchange networks can support treatment queries on an existing treatment relationship. Two providers treating the same patient are not business associates of each other, so no BAA is involved. Identifiable records are needed for treatment, so de-identification would defeat the purpose, and per-disclosure opt-in is not the general rule, though stricter rules such as Part 2 can still apply to some records.

q: A sending-side team plans to add a new optional segment to an outbound feed. Whom must it involve before go-live?
opts: No one outside the sending team, because HL7 v2 receivers must ignore unknown segments
Only the engine team, since the engine absorbs every format change that arrives
The receiving system's owners, since even an additive change can break their parser
Only compliance, since the new segment adds more PHI fields to the feed
why: Interfaces sit between two parties, and a change that seems additive can still break a receiver whose parser was not built to tolerate it, so the receiver is a required participant in testing. The standard encourages tolerance but cannot be relied on in every implementation. An engine cannot absorb a change the receiver rejects, and compliance review is a separate matter from technical compatibility.

q: Raising an MPI's match threshold generally reduces overlay errors but increases fragmented histories.
opts: True
False
why: A stricter threshold links fewer record pairs, so fewer different people get merged, but more records for the same person stay unlinked. Lowering it does the reverse. Tuning the threshold is therefore a trade-off between the two failure modes, and borderline scores are usually sent to a steward for review.

q: Which items belong in a change request for a live production interface? (Choose three.)
opts: A rollback plan
Sign-off from the owner of the receiving system
Skipping non-production testing for changes that touch only a single field
A plan for messages that queue while the interface is paused
Approval from the sending team alone, since it owns the change
why: A rollback plan, the receiving owner's agreement, and a plan for traffic during the pause are standard parts of change control. Single-field changes can still break a parser, so testing is not skipped. Approval from only one side ignores that the interface belongs to both.

q: Which statements about matching and stewardship in an MPI are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: Pairs scoring between the two thresholds are usually queued for a steward to review
Raising the auto-link threshold cuts false merges but may leave more duplicates unlinked
A merged record can never be unmerged once the link has been created in the MPI
Exact matching on MRN is enough across facilities because MRNs are globally unique
Probabilistic matching scores agreement across several demographic fields
why: Borderline scores go to human review, thresholds trade false merges against missed links, and probabilistic matching scores agreement across fields. Mature MPIs support unmerging because errors happen. MRNs are unique only within the issuing system, so exact MRN matching across facilities is unreliable.

q: Which arrangement requires a Business Associate Agreement?
opts: Sending a patient's records to a specialist who is treating that patient
Sending a patient's records to the app the patient chose to receive them
A cloud vendor hosting the engine's message archive, which contains PHI
Giving a university a dataset de-identified under Safe Harbor
why: A vendor that stores or handles PHI on the hospital's behalf is a business associate and needs a BAA. A specialist treating the same patient is another provider, not a vendor. An app the patient chose is acting for the patient, not for the hospital. De-identified data is no longer PHI, so sharing it does not create a business associate relationship.

q: Interface analysts who view PHI in an engine's message viewer are subject to the same access logging and minimum necessary expectations as clinicians.
opts: True
False
why: Message archives contain real patient data, so access to them is PHI access like any other. It should be role-limited to what troubleshooting needs, logged, and reviewed. Treating the engine console as exempt because it is technical tooling is a common compliance gap.

q: A research extract is being prepared under Safe Harbor. Which element would prevent it from qualifying as de-identified?
opts: The patient's state of residence
The year of admission
Exact admission dates, including the day
The first three digits of a ZIP code covering a large population
why: Safe Harbor requires removing date elements more specific than the year that are tied to an individual, so a full admission date fails. State-level geography and the year alone are permitted, as is the first three digits of a ZIP code when the area is sufficiently populous.

q: An HIE holds substance use disorder program records covered by 42 CFR Part 2. A clinician at another hospital runs a routine, non-emergency treatment query, and the patient has only a general HIE treatment opt-in. What should the HIE do?
opts: Release them, since the general treatment opt-in covers every category of data
Release them with the patient's names and direct identifiers removed
Withhold them unless the patient has given consent that meets Part 2's requirements
